title: Insecure Deserialization
summary: Insecure deserialization is a class of vulnerability that appears when an application rebuilds an object from data it did not fully trust, and that reconstruction step has side effects. In a serialized form, structured data is flattened into a byte stream or text string for storage or transport, and deserialization turns it back into live objects. The danger is that many runtimes do more than copy fields: they instantiate the named class, run constructors and hooks, and resolve references, so an attacker who controls the stream can name a class whose construction performs something dangerous. Practical impact ranges from logic tampering, where a hidden field such as a role or price is altered, to remote code execution when a gadget chain of existing library classes is invoked in sequence. It shows up in session stores, message queues, cached objects and API endpoints that accept native serialized formats. The common mistake is believing that signing or encrypting the payload makes it safe, which only proves origin; a trusted sender can still be manipulated, so the durable fix is to avoid native deserialization of untrusted input, restrict permitted types with an allowlist, and validate the resulting object.

beginner.definition: Serialization means turning a program object into a flat form, like text or bytes, so it can be saved or sent. Deserialization means turning that flat form back into a working object. Insecure deserialization is when a program does this with data from an untrusted source and does not check it. The word serialization is often shortened to ser and deserialization to deser.
beginner.whyItMatters: Rebuilding an object can run code inside the program, not just copy values. If an attacker controls the data, they may change hidden values such as a user role or a price. In bad cases they can make the program run their own instructions. This kind of flaw is easy to miss in review because the risky line looks like ordinary loading. The safe habit is to accept simple data and check it, not to rebuild complex objects from strangers.
howItWorks: A program creates an object, such as a user profile, and serializes it into a flat string or byte stream.
That flat form is stored in a file, a session store or a message queue, and later sent back to a program.
Deserialization reads the flat form and rebuilds the object, often naming the class it should create.
Many runtimes run constructor code and special hook methods while rebuilding, so extra actions can happen.
If an attacker can edit the flat form, they may change values or request a class with dangerous behaviour.
Controls include accepting only simple formats, restricting allowed types and checking the rebuilt object.
beginner.example: Think of a warehouse that receives sealed boxes with a label saying which machine to use. The staff never open the box. They just read the label and start the machine it names. Normally the machine packs the goods. Now imagine someone swaps the label for one that names the boiler room instead. The staff follow the label and start the boiler, and the warehouse fills with steam. Signing the box only proves who sent it, not that the label is wise to obey. The fix is to accept plain lists of items, read them carefully, and never start a machine just because a label asked.
takeaways: Rebuilding an object from data can trigger code, so treat it as a dangerous action.
Do not accept native serialized objects from users, files or queues you do not control.
Signing proves who sent the data, not that the data is safe to load.

objectives: Define serialization and deserialization and explain why the reverse step can be dangerous.
Describe how controlling a serialized payload can lead to logic tampering or code execution.
Recognise where untrusted serialized data appears, including session stores, queues and API parameters.
Explain why integrity checks such as signing do not remove the underlying risk.
List defensive options, including simple data formats, type allowlists and validation of rebuilt objects.
